title: Ballet Shoes
author: Noel Streatfeild
short_summary: Three unrelated orphan girls — Pauline, Petrova, and Posy Fossil — are all brought home as babies by an eccentric fossil-collector known as Great-Uncle Matthew. Raised by his great-niece Sylvia and their devoted nurse, the three sisters attend a school for dancing and acting, each discovering a very different talent, and each determined to make the name Fossil mean something of their own.
extended_summary:
Great-Uncle Matthew, an adventurous fossil collector nicknamed GUM, has a habit of bringing home unusual souvenirs from his travels — but his strangest finds are three baby girls, each rescued under different circumstances and given the same last name, Fossil, so they can grow up as sisters. When GUM sets off on another long expedition and doesn't come back for years, it falls to his great-niece Sylvia and their loyal nurse Nana to raise Pauline, Petrova, and Posy on a shrinking budget.

To make ends meet, Sylvia takes in boarders, and the boarders change everything: two retired professors teach the girls their lessons for nothing, a dance teacher gets them into the Children's Academy, and a garage owner gives Petrova somewhere to be happy. At the Academy the three turn out to be completely different. Pauline is a natural actress and is on the stage as soon as the law allows; Posy is a dancer of real genius; and Petrova, who would rather be under a car than on a stage, works at it anyway because the family needs the money.

Every birthday the three swear the same vow: to put the name Fossil into the history books, because it is their own and nobody can say they inherited it. By the end each of them has a way to try — Pauline to a film in Hollywood, Posy to a great ballet teacher abroad, and Petrova to the engines and aeroplanes she has wanted all along, once GUM finally comes home.

questions.prompt: The Fossil girls do not go out to school. Who teaches them their lessons instead?

options: Two retired professors who board in the house
Sylvia, who had been a teacher before they came
Nana, in the evenings after the day's work
The Academy, as part of the dancing timetable

questions.explanation: Doctor Jakes and Doctor Smith — one a professor of literature, the other of mathematics — offer to teach the girls for nothing in return for their rooms. The house paying its way with lodgers is not just background: almost every good thing that happens to the Fossils arrives through a boarder.

questions.prompt: Why are three unrelated babies all given the surname Fossil?

options: It is a name of their own that no ancestor gave them
It was the name on the ship that brought them to England
It was Great-Uncle Matthew's own family name
Nana chose it so the neighbours would stop asking

questions.explanation: GUM collects fossils, so a fossil is what each foundling becomes. The joke turns serious in the vow the girls repeat every birthday: because nobody handed them the name, anything they make it mean will be genuinely theirs.

questions.prompt: Every birthday the three sisters repeat their vow: to try to put the name Fossil into the ___ books, because it is their very own.
questions.explanation: The second half of the vow is the important half: nobody can say they got there because of their grandfathers. Three children with no family at all turn that into an advantage — whatever they achieve cannot be inherited.

questions.prompt: One of the boarders becomes Petrova's particular friend. What does he have that makes her so happy?

options: A car and a garage where she can help
A workshop full of clocks to take apart
A library of books about famous flights
A camera she is allowed to borrow

questions.explanation: Mr. Simpson lets Petrova into the garage and under the bonnet, and it is the only place in the book where she is straightforwardly happy. It matters later: the adult who takes her interests seriously is not her teacher or her guardian, but a lodger with a car.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the Fossils' stage career in the order they happen.

items: A dance teacher lodging in the house suggests the Academy
The three sisters start classes at Madame Fidolia's
Pauline appears on stage in The Blue Bird
Pauline is given the leading part in Alice in Wonderland
Pauline's understudy is sent on in her place
Posy leaves to study with a great teacher abroad

questions.explanation: Nothing here is luck except the first step. Theo Dane happens to lodge in the house; everything after that the girls work for, and the one time Pauline behaves as though the theatre owes her something, she is taken out of her own part for an evening.

questions.prompt: Match each grown-up to what they do for the Fossil girls.

right: Teaches them literature in exchange for her room
Brings them into the Academy in the first place
Runs the Academy, and teaches one of them privately
Lets one of them work on an engine in his garage

questions.explanation: Sylvia cannot afford any of this. Every one of these adults gives the girls something for nothing — which is why the book keeps insisting, quietly, that the Fossils owe their chances to people who chose to help them.

questions.prompt: Two of the sisters are as unlike as possible. Sort each detail by which one it belongs to.

options.label: Happiest with her hands inside an engine
Reads everything she can find about flying
Dreads every audition she has to attend
Was left as a baby with a pair of ballet shoes
Is taught privately by the head of the Academy
Thinks of almost nothing except dancing

questions.explanation: The book refuses to make the three sisters into one kind of child. Posy's single-mindedness would be selfishness in anyone without her gift, and Petrova's misery on stage is treated as a real cost — not as something she should cheer up about.

questions.prompt: Pauline is doing well in a leading part when the management sends her understudy on instead of her for a performance. Why?

options: Success had gone to her head and she had grown rude
She had lost her voice and could not be heard
The understudy's family had complained to the theatre
Her licence to perform had run out that week

questions.explanation: She begins behaving as though the production could not manage without her — so for one night it does. It is the sharpest lesson in the book, and Pauline never forgets it: being talented is not the same as being owed anything.

questions.prompt: Petrova trains for the stage and goes to auditions for years, even though she hates performing and would much rather be working on engines. Was it fair to expect her to keep going? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both sides can score full marks. A strong 'not fair' answer notices that nobody asks Petrova what she wants, that she is miserable, and that talent is being demanded of a child who has a different one. A strong 'fair' answer notices that the household genuinely needed the money, that her sisters were working too, and that Petrova herself chooses to keep going rather than let them down. Accept either, with a reason from the book.

questions.prompt: At the end of the book the three sisters are heading in three different directions, and Great-Uncle Matthew has finally come home. Write a short letter from one of them to GUM, telling him what she is doing now and whether she thinks the Fossil vow is coming true.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong letter picks one sister, says something that actually fits her — a film, a ballet school, an aeroplane — and takes a position on the vow, either that she is on her way or that she is nowhere near yet. A letter that could have been written by any of the three is weaker.

questions.prompt: The girls do not call Sylvia by her name or 'Aunt'. Because she is their guardian, they call her ___.
questions.explanation: It is short for Guardian, and it is exactly the sort of name children invent for a relationship that has no proper word. Sylvia is not their mother, aunt or sister, and the made-up name quietly admits it while making her theirs anyway.

questions.prompt: Madame Fidolia does something for Posy that she does for none of the other pupils at the Academy. What is it?

options: She gives her private lessons herself
She lets her perform before she is twelve
She pays the family for Posy's training
She puts her straight into the senior class

questions.explanation: Madame Fidolia, who was a great dancer herself, recognises that Posy is not merely good but exceptional, and teaches her alone. It sets up the ending: Posy's gift is big enough to take her away from her sisters, and everyone can see it long before she goes.
